description: Five visitor-accessible rounds in Fife, Scotland: the Old Course at St Andrews, modern classic Kingsbarns, the new daily-fee links at Dumbarnie, the periscope starter's hut at Elie, and Old Tom Morris's Balcomie Links at Crail.
intro: Fife is the county where golf began, and it is still the best place on earth to plan a golf trip: the Home of Golf sits at its center, and within a short drive in either direction there are world-class links that welcome visitors. Everything on this list is bookable without a membership, from a course that has hosted The Open more times than any other to a 200-year-old club where the starter checks the first fairway through a submarine periscope. Base in St Andrews or in one of the East Neuk fishing villages, allow at least four or five days, and book the big names months ahead.

sections.heading: 1. The Old Course, St Andrews
paragraphs: There is no more famous tee time in golf. The Old Course at St Andrews is public linksland, owned by the town and managed by the St Andrews Links Trust, and it has hosted The Open Championship more times than any other course. Its landmarks are golf's shared vocabulary: the Swilcan Bridge over the burn on the 1st and 18th, the Road Hole 17th with its blind tee shot over the Old Course Hotel, seven double greens, and the vast, flat expanse that makes the course look deceptively simple until the wind gets up. A valid handicap certificate is required to play, with a maximum handicap of 36.

Most visitors get on through the daily ballot, a lottery run by the Links Trust: groups of two to four enter by 2pm two days before play, with results published later that afternoon, and solo golfers use a separate singles draw the day before. Roughly half of each day's tee times go through the ballot, so it is a genuinely realistic route — but build your trip so the Old Course is a hope, not the plan: book Kingsbarns or Dumbarnie as your anchors and enter the ballot every day you are in town. There is no play on Sundays, when the links rests and opens to walkers, and a caddie is strongly recommended on a first visit because the lines off many tees are not the lines a yardage book suggests.

sections.heading: 2. Kingsbarns Golf Links, Kingsbarns
paragraphs: Six miles south of St Andrews, Kingsbarns is the modern classic that proves a new course can feel ancient. American architect Kyle Phillips, working with Mark Parsinen, shaped it from relatively flat farmland and opened it in 2000, moving hundreds of thousands of tonnes of earth to build dunes that look as if the sea put them there. It co-hosts the Alfred Dunhill Links Championship alongside the Old Course and Carnoustie, hosted the Women's British Open in 2017, and an astonishing 17 of its 18 holes offer direct views of the North Sea. It is a daily-fee course, open to visitors on weekdays and weekends through the season.

Kingsbarns is the simple win on a Fife trip: no ballot, no lottery, just a tee time booked directly with the club, with next-season times released from 1 June each year. It closes over winter for turf protection, running roughly late March to early November, so plan it inside that window. Book well ahead for peak summer — it sells out — and request a caddie when you book, as they are independent contractors and worth having on a first visit. The clubhouse sits about 15 minutes' drive from St Andrews, so it pairs easily with the Old, New, or Jubilee courses on the same trip.

sections.heading: 3. Dumbarnie Links, Upper Largo
paragraphs: Dumbarnie is Fife's newest links and its most visitor-friendly: a high-end public course, open for daily-fee play with no members' club at all. Designed by former Ryder Cup player Clive Clark and opened in May 2020 on 345 acres of the Balcarres Estate, it runs along a mile and a half of shoreline on the north side of the Firth of Forth, with sea views from all 18 holes. The routing breaks with links tradition — two big loops with elevated tees facing into the Forth instead of the classic out-and-back — and it is already tournament-proven, having hosted the Women's Scottish Open in 2021.

Because there is no membership to work around, booking is straightforward: tee times are available by phone or email, and booking two to three months ahead is prudent for peak summer. The course plays from about 5,300 to 7,600 yards across five sets of tees, so choose your tees honestly — the risk-reward par 4s, including a driveable 5th with a narrow left fairway, are far more fun from a yardage you can actually score from. It sits about 11 miles from St Andrews, making it an easy second anchor on a trip built around the Old Course ballot, and the clubhouse, known as The Old Barn, sits 80 feet above sea level with views down the 1st and 18th.

sources.title: Dumbarnie Links: Clive Clark on Scotland's new golf course — National Club Golfer

sections.heading: 4. The Golf House Club, Elie
paragraphs: Elie is the quirkiest round in Fife, and five-time Open champion Peter Thomson called it the most enjoyable course he knew. Golf has been played on the Earlsferry links since at least 1589, when a royal charter gave villagers permission to use the land; the current 18 holes were largely laid out by Old Tom Morris in 1895, with revisions by James Braid, who was born in Earlsferry and learned the game here. The opening hole is a blind drive over a hill, and the starter checks the fairway is clear by peering through a periscope salvaged from the Royal Navy submarine HMS Excalibur — a ritual no first-time visitor forgets.

Visitor access is limited in summer because members get priority, so book early and aim for weekdays; the club is about 30 minutes' drive from St Andrews on the East Neuk coast. At just over 6,200 yards from the back tees it suits every level of player, and a late or twilight round is a good way in when the sheet is tight. Arrive early enough to watch the periscope ritual at the first tee, and pair Elie with Crail or Lundin Links the same day — the East Neuk villages are close together, and the drive between them along the Firth of Forth is part of the trip.

sections.heading: 5. Crail Golfing Society — Balcomie Links, Crail
paragraphs: Crail Golfing Society, founded in 1786, is the seventh-oldest golf club in the world, and its Balcomie Links is one of Scotland's true gems. Old Tom Morris laid out the course in 1895 on rugged, hilly linksland above the North Sea, and it remains a short, endlessly varied test — around 5,359 metres from the back tees — where the wind, not the length, is the defense. The club is famously welcoming to visitors, and the Balcomie clubhouse, with its restaurant and spike bar overlooking the sea, has a reputation for friendliness and good food to match the golf.

Visitors are welcome on weekdays and weekends but must book in advance, and a handicap is required. The society has two 18-hole courses, so a day ticket covering a round on Balcomie and a round on the newer Craighead Links makes a natural 36-hole day. Note the winter arrangement: from November to March only one of the two courses is open midweek, switching fortnightly, so check which is in play before you travel in the off-season. Crail sits about 30 minutes south of St Andrews in the East Neuk, and it pairs perfectly with Elie as a quieter, cheaper counterweight to the St Andrews headliners.
